quiz.why: Gravity supplies the centripetal force.

quiz.q: At 400 km a spacecraft orbits Earth about every…
quiz.why: ≈ 92.4 minutes.

quiz.q: A Hohmann transfer uses…
quiz.why: One at each end of the transfer ellipse.

quiz.q: Geostationary radius ≈
quiz.why: Kepler’s third law with one sidereal day.

quiz.q: Astronauts float because there is no gravity in orbit.
quiz.why: At 400 km gravity is about 89% of its surface value; they are in free fall.

quiz.q: To catch a spacecraft ahead of you, just speed up.
quiz.why: Speeding up raises your orbit and lowers your angular rate.

quiz.q: Higher orbits need more speed.
quiz.why: Circular speed falls with height, though reaching higher orbits takes more total Δv.

quiz.q: Find the speed and period of a circular orbit 400 km up. Give your answer in km/s.
quiz.why: 7.67 km/s and ≈ 92.4 minutes.

quiz.q: Find the geostationary radius. Give your answer in km.
quiz.why: ≈ 42,164 km from Earth’s center (about 35,786 km above the equator).

quiz.q: Find the Hohmann Δv from a 300 km circular orbit to geostationary radius. Give your answer in km/s.
quiz.why: Total ≈ 3.90 km/s; transfer ≈ 5.27 hours (ignoring any plane change).

quiz.q: Find v for a circular orbit at r = 7,000 km. Give your answer in m/s.
T ∝ r^(3/2): 8 times longer.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit. If the orbit radius quadruples, how does the period change?

quiz.q: They stay over one spot and can image the same hemisphere continuously.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit. Why are many weather satellites geostationary?

quiz.q: Climate monitoring depends on orbit choice. Sun-synchronous orbits let Landsat image the same place under similar lighting, so changes in forests, crops and ice stand out, while geostationary weather satellites watch storms develop continuously.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: Orbits also need care: debris threatens these missions, so spacecraft are increasingly designed to be disposed of at the end of their lives.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: In a circular orbit gravity supplies the centripetal force: v = √(μ/r), with μ = GM.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: Kepler’s third law: T = 2π√(a³/μ). Higher orbits are slower and take longer.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: A geostationary orbit has a period of one sidereal day (86,164 s) and sits over the equator at a radius of about 42,164 km.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: A Hohmann transfer uses two burns along an ellipse that touches both circular orbits; it is the most efficient two-burn transfer between coplanar circular orbits.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: Low Earth orbit (about 400 km for the ISS), sun-synchronous polar orbits for imaging, and geostationary orbit for weather each serve different missions.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.
